left.label: SIGN AND LIVE
left.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, seated at a small table in a dark stone-and-timber jail cell at dawn, straw on the floor, a barred window, his hand hovering a quill pen over a single sheet of paper

right.label: REFUSE AND HANG
right.subject: an empty noose rope hanging from a bare timber beam against a cold grey dawn sky over a rocky hill outside Salem in 1692, no people

storyboard.claim: Proctor's last choice: sign a lie and live, or refuse and hang.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Split choice: Proctor's hand over the confession paper in the jail cell vs. the empty noose on Gallows Hill at dawn — the two outcomes side by side.
storyboard.onScreenText: SIGN AND LIVE / REFUSE AND HANG
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the jail-dawn sequence (same cell, same paper) set up in 162: the paper he has just signed is now framed as one side of a choice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the two prices: a lie to a corrupt state vs. the rope.

image.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, seated at a small table in a dark stone-and-timber jail cell at dawn holding a signed sheet of paper, while the haggard young clergyman in black kneels on the straw and grips his forearm, pleading

storyboard.claim: Proctor signs, and a guilt-broken Hale begs him to lie and live.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Hale on his knees in the cell clutching Proctor's arm while Proctor holds the signed paper — the minister physically pleading for the lie.
storyboard.onScreenText: HALE: LIFE IS GOD'S MOST PRECIOUS GIFT
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same jail cell and same paper: the choice from 163 now has a voice pulling toward 'sign'.
storyboard.addedInformation: Hale, the man who started the hunt, is now the one urging the lie.

image.subject: a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, holding up a signed sheet of paper in one hand and pointing out through an open jail doorway toward the plain weathered timber door of a Puritan meetinghouse across a grey dawn yard, a hammer and iron nail resting on the table beside him

storyboard.claim: Danforth demands the signed confession be nailed to the church door.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Danforth brandishing the signed paper and pointing toward the meetinghouse door, hammer and nail on the table — the public display he wants.
storyboard.onScreenText: NAIL IT TO THE CHURCH DOOR
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The same signed paper changes hands: from Proctor's private surrender to Danforth's public trophy.
storyboard.addedInformation: The confession is not enough for Danforth; he wants it posted for the whole village.

image.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, standing in a dark stone-and-timber jail cell at dawn and ripping a signed sheet of paper in half with both fists, his face contorted, torn pieces falling toward the straw floor

storyboard.claim: Realising his signature will justify the hangings, Proctor tears the confession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor ripping the signed paper in two — the paper that was going on the church door is destroyed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the sequence: the paper signed in 162-164 and claimed by Danforth in 165 is torn apart.
storyboard.addedInformation: His name would be used to justify hanging the others.

storyboard.claim: Proctor cries 'because it is my name' as Elizabeth watches and Hale pleads with her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation: the line itself is the climax; the torn paper image from 166 has just carried the action.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The words behind the act of 166 — why he tore it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The play's title idea in Proctor's own words.

image.subject: a composed Puritan wife in her thirties, brown hair hidden under a white linen coif, dark blue wool dress with a plain white collar and apron, restrained grave expression, Salem 1692, at the barred window of a dark jail at dawn, tears on her face, hands folded firmly, turning away from the young clergyman in black who reaches toward her pleading, an oxcart waiting outside

storyboard.claim: Elizabeth refuses to stop John: 'He have his goodness now.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth at the jail window turning away from Hale's outstretched hands while the cart waits outside — she will not pull John back.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the jail-dawn stage: the plea Hale made to John (164) is now aimed at Elizabeth and refused.
storyboard.addedInformation: Elizabeth chooses to let him die whole rather than live broken.

image.subject: a composed Puritan wife in her thirties, brown hair hidden under a white linen coif, dark blue wool dress with a plain white collar and apron, restrained grave expression, Salem 1692, visibly pregnant, one hand on her belly, sitting alone on a plank bench in the dim common room of a 1692 Puritan farmhouse beside a wide hearth fire, two small pairs of boys' boots and a man's empty chair at the plain plank table

storyboard.claim: Objection: they have children and she is pregnant — shouldn't she beg him to live?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pregnant Elizabeth by the hearth with the children's boots and John's empty chair — the family his death will leave behind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the jail to the home it will empty — the cost side of Proctor's choice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the case against Proctor: a father abandoning his family.

storyboard.claim: Is tearing up the confession deeply selfish? The host vehemently disagrees.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question: the debate itself is the shape here.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the objection raised over the image in 169 as a direct question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the counter-argument that follows.

left.label: MODERN LENS
left.subject: a modern American father in a casual sweater at a kitchen table in 2020s suburbia holding his young son on his lap, warm daylight

right.label: PURITAN LENS
right.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, standing upright in a dark stone-and-timber jail cell at dawn, hand on an open Bible on the small table, face resolved

storyboard.claim: Judging Proctor with a secular 21st-century lens misses what Elizabeth understands.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Modern father valuing survival with family vs. Proctor with his hand on the Bible valuing his soul — two value systems side by side.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question of 170 by contrasting the viewer's frame with the 1692 one.
storyboard.addedInformation: The objection comes from our era's values, not theirs.

storyboard.claim: For John, survival without moral integrity is worse than death.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only statement: an abstract value claim where any picture would only repeat 171.
storyboard.onScreenText: SURVIVAL WITHOUT INTEGRITY IS WORSE THAN DEATH
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the sentence begun in 171 — what Elizabeth understands.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the Puritan scale of values plainly.

image.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, standing in the doorway of a 1692 Puritan farmhouse unable to meet the gaze of his two young sons on the threshold, while behind him across the field a signed paper is nailed to the weathered timber door of the village meetinghouse

storyboard.claim: Letting the lie be nailed up would make him complicit in his friends' deaths; he couldn't face his sons.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor turning his eyes from his sons on the doorstep while his confession hangs nailed to the meetinghouse door in the distance — the shame that a lived life would carry.
storyboard.onScreenText: HOW DO YOU FACE YOUR SONS?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pictures the alternative future: what 'surviving' (172) would have cost him.
storyboard.addedInformation: The confession would betray Rebecca, Martha and the other condemned.

image.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, seen from behind riding upright in an oxcart up a dirt track on a rocky hill outside Salem at grey dawn, a crowd of townsfolk watching, first light breaking over the ridge

storyboard.claim: He chooses the gallows because he finally understands the price of a name.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor upright in the oxcart climbing Gallows Hill at dawn — the chosen death shown as the journey, not the act.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the whole jail sequence: the torn paper (166) leads to the cart on the hill.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ending of the play; closes the story before the history section.

left.label: REAL ABIGAIL: ~11
left.subject: a small eleven-year-old Puritan girl with dark hair under a white linen cap and a plain grey wool dress, standing beside a wooden chair in a 1692 parsonage room, ordinary daylight

right.label: REAL PROCTOR: 60
right.subject: a white-haired sixty-year-old Puritan tavern keeper and farmer with a lined face and grey beard, plain brown coat, standing in a 1692 farmyard

storyboard.claim: Miller made changes: the real Abigail was about 11, Proctor was 60, and there was no affair.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The real ages side by side — a child and an old man — which makes the affair impossible at a glance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Steps out of the play into history; starts the Miller sequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: The historical facts behind the fiction.

image.subject: a manual typewriter on a wooden desk in a 1950s study, a typed page in the roller, old books about the Salem witch trials open beside it, a pair of horn-rimmed glasses resting on them

storyboard.claim: Miller changed history for a reason; he wrote it in 1953.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Miller at his typewriter with Salem trial books open beside him and a newspaper — the 1690s source and the 1950s present on one desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Miller sequence: from the facts he changed (175) to the man changing them.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Miller and the date of writing.

image.subject: a 1950s wood-panelled government hearing room, a panel of stern men in suits behind a long raised table with microphones, a single witness at a small table facing them, flashbulb cameras, black-and-white documentary photograph

storyboard.claim: The play is an allegory for the McCarthy hearings and HUAC.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The HUAC hearing room: raised committee, lone witness — the Salem courtroom's 1950s twin.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Miller's desk (176) to what he was writing about.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the real target of the allegory.

left.label: 1692: TITUBA NAMES
left.subject: a Black woman in her forties from Barbados, dark skin, a faded red headscarf, a coarse brown wool dress and shawl, Salem 1692, on her knees in a candlelit parsonage room pointing a trembling finger while a gaunt middle-aged Puritan minister in a plain black coat and white preaching bands, thinning dark hair, anxious pinched face, Salem Village 1692, leans over her

right.label: 1952: KAZAN NAMES
right.subject: a 1950s man in a dark suit at a small witness table with a microphone in a wood-panelled hearing room, reading aloud from a sheet of paper toward a panel behind a raised table

storyboard.claim: Truth got you blacklisted, naming names got you forgiven; Kazan did what Tituba did.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tituba pointing out names under Parris's pressure vs. a 1950s director reading names into the microphone — the same act three centuries apart.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Holds the hearing room from 177 and sets the Salem original beside it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Elia Kazan as the modern Tituba; same reward structure.

image.subject: a tall lean American playwright in his late thirties with dark wavy hair and black horn-rimmed glasses, a 1950s grey suit and narrow tie, 1950s America, seated alone at a small witness table with microphones in a wood-panelled 1950s hearing room, arms folded and jaw set, a panel of men at a raised table facing him

storyboard.claim: Miller himself was called before the committee and refused to name names.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Miller at the witness table, arms folded, facing the dais — the playwright in Proctor's position.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same hearing room as 177-178; now the lone witness is Miller, and he refuses.
storyboard.addedInformation: Miller lived his own play in 1956.

left.label: PROCTOR, 1692
left.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, standing before judges at a raised bench in the Salem courtroom, refusing, a torn paper on the floor at his feet

right.label: MILLER, 1956
right.subject: a tall lean American playwright in his late thirties with dark wavy hair and black horn-rimmed glasses, a 1950s grey suit and narrow tie, 1950s America, standing at a witness table in a wood-panelled 1950s hearing room, one hand raised, refusing to answer the panel at the raised table

storyboard.claim: Miller made Proctor's refusal his own — and that raises a tough question.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor before the Salem bench and Miller before the committee in matching stances — the same refusal in two centuries.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the Miller sequence: the writer and his hero merge before the critique begins.
storyboard.addedInformation: Bridges into the critique of Miller's changes.

storyboard.claim: By making a teenager's sexual jealousy the engine, does Miller distort the real victims?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question: the critique is posed as a direct question.
storyboard.onScreenText: DOES THE PLAY DISTORT THE REAL VICTIMS?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the critique sequence announced in 180.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the charge against Miller's fiction.

image.subject: a row of plain weathered fieldstone markers in the tall grass of a New England hillside at grey dawn, a single white linen cap lying on one stone, bare trees behind, Massachusetts

storyboard.claim: Does the allegory rob the real victims of their truth? A vital critique.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bare stone markers of the real dead on a hillside, a white cap left on one — the actual people behind the fiction.
storyboard.onScreenText: DOES IT ROB THEM OF THEIR TRUTH?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pictures the 'real victims' asked about in 181.
storyboard.addedInformation: Twenty real people died; the critique speaks for them.

image.subject: a heavy-set wealthy Puritan landowner in his forties, florid face, grey-streaked hair, a fine dark green wool coat with pewter buttons and a wide-brimmed black hat, Salem 1692, standing at a split-rail fence with his hand on a rolled land deed, gazing across ploughed fields toward a distant farmhouse, while behind him the periwigged judge, and the gaunt Puritan minister in black, stand together on the road

storyboard.claim: The real terror: state and church colluded to kill neighbours over mundane things like land — no love triangle needed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Putnam's eyes and hand on the neighbour's fields with the judge and the minister standing behind him — land greed backed by court and church.
storyboard.onScreenText: STATE + CHURCH KILLED NEIGHBORS OVER LAND
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the critique: what the love-triangle hides (182's victims died for this).
storyboard.addedInformation: The true engine was land and institutional collusion, not jealousy.

image.subject: an empty 1950s Broadway theatre stage under a single spotlight, a plain wooden Puritan chair at its centre, rows of red velvet seats in shadow

storyboard.claim: Fiction needs a human focal point to make systemic failure felt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A gripped 1953 audience, a hand to the mouth — the play making the terror felt, the payoff of Miller's focus.
storyboard.onScreenText: FICTION MAKES YOU FEEL THE TERROR
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The defence answering 183: the human story is how the system's failure reaches an audience.
storyboard.addedInformation: Why Miller's distortion still serves a purpose.

image.subject: the Salem 1692 courtroom in the meetinghouse, judges at a raised bench in black robes, crowded benches, high rafters, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, sliding a land deed across the bench to a kneeling woman who has just signed a confession, while a court clerk stacks arrest warrants beside him, calm and orderly

storyboard.claim: Salem wasn't hysteria but an airtight system of rational incentives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A calm, orderly court transaction: confession signed, deed handed back, warrants stacked — the machine running, not a mob raving.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the synthesis sequence; returns to the courtroom as the system itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Restates the video's thesis.

storyboard.claim: A system that pays people to lie will always find liars.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline: the thesis line deserves the whole screen.
storyboard.onScreenText: A SYSTEM THAT PAYS PEOPLE TO LIE WILL ALWAYS FIND LIARS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The rule distilled from the courtroom machine of 185.
storyboard.addedInformation: The video's central lesson in one line.

image.subject: a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, standing alone and upright in a dark stone-and-timber jail cell at dawn, the torn halves of a signed paper on the straw at his feet, first light from the barred window falling on his face

storyboard.claim: The only defence is the individual who refuses to sell their integrity — like Proctor.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor standing upright in the dawn light over the torn confession — the one man who would not sell his name.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the synthesis back to the torn paper of 166 as the answer to the system of 185-186.
storyboard.addedInformation: Proctor as the model of individual refusal.

storyboard.claim: Final thought: look at the incentive structures in your own life.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only address to the viewer; the turn from Salem to 'you'.
storyboard.onScreenText: LOOK AT THE INCENTIVES IN YOUR OWN LIFE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the lesson of 187 onto the viewer; starts the closing sequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Moves from analysis to the viewer's own life.

image.subject: a modern office worker in a shirt and tie sitting across a glass conference table from a manager, a single printed form and a pen pushed toward him, colleagues visible through the glass wall behind him at their desks, cold fluorescent light, present day

storyboard.claim: Imagine a system that rewards you for betraying your colleagues.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A modern worker being pushed a paper and pen while his colleagues sit visible behind the glass — Proctor's signed paper in a modern office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same closing sequence: the abstract 'your life' of 188 becomes a concrete modern room.
storyboard.addedInformation: Translates the Salem bargain into today's workplace.

image.subject: close view of a man's hand in a modern shirt cuff hovering a pen over the signature line of a single printed sheet on a glass conference table, the pen not yet touching the paper, cold fluorescent light, present day

storyboard.claim: If your livelihood were threatened for refusing, what choice would you make?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The pen hovering, unsigned, over the modern form — the same moment Proctor faced at the jail table, left open for the viewer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the closing sequence: the office scene of 189 narrows to the hand over the paper, echoing Proctor's quill in 163.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ends on the viewer's own unsigned decision.
